interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the reading bar climb to meet the design's 0.436 Ω at 70 °C, when you drag the cable's temperature up from the 20 °C test day.
interactive.title: One cable, two temperatures
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
There are thirteen screens, with Back and Continue. They check the showroom's readings against its design, then hand it over.

Screen 1, Do you still have it? The question: “Remember the immersion heater circuit: 15 m of 1.5 mm² line and cpc. Its design R1+R2 is 24.2 × 1.2 × 15 ÷ 1000 = 0.436 Ω. You test it once it is installed, cold, on a 20 °C day. What should it read if the cable is as designed?” There are three choices, in this order: “0.436 Ω: the design figure”, “0.363 Ω: 24.2 × 15 ÷ 1000” and “0.523 Ω: 0.436 × 1.2”. Right: “Still there.” Then the working. The 1.2 takes the cable from 20 °C up to its running temperature. A cold test leaves it out: 24.2 × 15 ÷ 1000 = 0.363 Ω. A last line names the two slips: 0.436 Ω is the hot figure, and 0.523 Ω warms it twice. Then come two buttons. Refresh the why goes to screen 2. Skip to the practice goes to screen 6. Wrong, 0.436 Ω: “That is the hot figure. The cable is cold when you test it, so it reads lower.” Wrong, 0.523 Ω: “That warms it twice. The 1.2 is already in 0.436 Ω.” Then the right working, and on to screen 2.

Screen 2, What it is for. “The design predicts what each circuit should read. Verification checks the installation against those figures before anyone uses it. It also checks each reading against its device's limit. So the designer hands the inspector the figures to test against, worked for the temperature of the test. Then the client gets the certificate and the records to run the building safely.” In red, what goes wrong if it is skipped: “Set a cold reading against a hot figure and it looks better than it is. It can pass a circuit that would fail when warm.[^1]”

Screen 3, The why: one cable, two temperatures. The picture: two bars for the heater's R1+R2. The first bar, Design, stands at 0.436 Ω, worked for the cable running at 70 °C. The second bar, Reading, is what the same cable reads at the slider's temperature. A thermometer beside them marks three temperatures. The maximum measured Zs values are set at 10 °C. The resistance tables are set at 20 °C. At 70 °C the cable is running hot. A slider sets the cable temperature, from 0 to 70 °C in steps of 1 °C. It opens on 20 °C. Two readouts show the factor from 20 °C, to 2 places, and the reading in Ω, to 3 places. The rule beside it: “Copper's resistance rises in step with its temperature plus 230 °C. So reading = 0.363 × (t + 230) ÷ 250.”

What he sees. At 20 °C the reading is 0.363 Ω, 0.073 Ω under the design. As the temperature rises, the reading climbs. At 70 °C the factor is 300 ÷ 250 = 1.20, and the reading meets the design at 0.436 Ω. At 10 °C the reading falls to 0.348 Ω. The words under it: “Nothing about the cable changed. Only its temperature did. So compare a reading with the design only at one temperature. The same rule gives the factors you use for R1+R2 and Zs. From 20 °C up to 90 °C it is 320 ÷ 250 = 1.28. From 20 °C down to a 15 °C test day it is 245 ÷ 250 = 0.98. The maximum measured Zs is the limit for a reading taken cold. It is the Table 41.3 figure divided by 1.25. That is 300 ÷ 240, from 70 °C down to 10 °C. So a cold reading should stay under 80% of the Table 41.3 figure. The 80% covers Ze too, though Ze does not warm with the cable. So the limit errs on the safe side.” The prompt above the picture: “Drag the temperature up to 70 °C.” Read: at 20 °C the cable reads 0.363 Ω. At 70 °C the same cable reads 0.436 Ω, the design's figure. Still: 70 °C.

Screen 4, Check. “A 6 A type C circuit's limit for a reading at 10 °C is 2.91 Ω. You test it on a 25 °C day. What is the most it may read?” There are three choices: “3.085 Ω: 2.91 × 1.06”, “2.745 Ω: 2.91 ÷ 1.06” and “3.64 Ω: the Table 41.3 figure”. Right, the first: “A warmer cable reads higher, so the limit rises with it. The factor from 10 °C is (25 + 230) ÷ (10 + 230) = 1.06. Then 2.91 × 1.06 = 3.085 Ω.” Wrong, the second: “That moves the limit the wrong way. A warmer day raises the reading, so it raises the limit too.” Wrong, the third: “3.64 Ω is the limit for the cable running hot. At 25 °C the cable is still far cooler than that.”

Screen 5, Worked example: the heater, as built, a line at each press. The prompt: “Work each step yourself first, then press Show.” Said once: “The heater circuit: Ze 0.21 Ω, 15 m of 1.5 mm² line and cpc at 24.2 mΩ/m, and a device whose Table 41.3 maximum is 2.73 Ω. The design gave R1+R2 0.436 Ω and Zs 0.646 Ω, both hot. You test on a 20 °C day.” The lines: Expected R1+R2 = 24.2 × 15 ÷ 1000 = 0.363 Ω. Expected Zs = 0.21 + 0.363 = 0.573 Ω. Limit at 10 °C = 2.73 ÷ 1.25 = 2.184 Ω. Factor from 10 °C to 20 °C = 250 ÷ 240 = 1.04. Limit on the day = 2.184 × 1.04 = 2.271 Ω. A note under the lines: “Expect a reading near 0.573 Ω, often a little under. It passes while it stays under 2.271 Ω. You may remember the design as 0.43 Ω and 0.64 Ω. Those are the same hot figures, cut to two places.” Read: on a 20 °C day the heater should read about 0.573 Ω, and the most it may read is 2.271 Ω.

Screen 6, Section A, question 4 (a). The scenario panel shows, with parts 3(g) and 3(i) carried forward. Zs at DBL2 is 0.392 Ω. Zs at C7's farthest bollard is 1.129 Ω. Said once: “Parts 3(g) and 3(i) are both worked hot. Assume the tests are done on a 15 °C day. Take that as a practice value. On a real job, record the day's temperature. At 20 °C the submain's core is 4.61 mΩ/m and its armour 6.8 mΩ/m, over 20.0 m. C7's 1.5 mm² line and cpc are 24.2 mΩ/m over its 23.8 m.” The question: “(a) Determine the earth fault loop impedance you expect at C7's farthest bollard on the test day.” A typed answer, part 4a. Factor from 20 °C = (15 + 230) ÷ (20 + 230) = 0.98. Submain = (4.61 + 6.8) × 20.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.228 Ω, and 0.228 × 0.98 = 0.223 Ω. C7 = 24.2 × 23.8 ÷ 1000 = 0.576 Ω, and 0.576 × 0.98 = 0.564 Ω. Zs = 0.1 + 0.223 + 0.564 = 0.887 Ω. Accepted too: 0.888 Ω, from unrounded working. Slips: 1.129 Ω, “That is the design's hot figure. The test is cold, so expect less.” 0.904 Ω, “Those are the 20 °C values. The test day is 15 °C, so multiply each by 0.98.” 0.787 Ω, “Add Ze, 0.1 Ω. The supply is part of the loop.” After two misses, the working. Then: “This is the figure you hand the inspector. The design's 1.129 Ω is the same circuit, hot.”

Screen 7, Section A, question 4 (b). Part 4(a) carried forward. Said once: “These as-built readings are practice examples, not measurements. Ze at the MDB: 0.08 Ω. R1+R2 of the submain: 0.214 Ω. R1+R2 of C7: 0.548 Ω. Zs read directly: 0.275 Ω at DBL2, 0.790 Ω at the farthest bollard. The submain's 10 A type C breaker has a Table 41.3 maximum of 2.19 Ω. Its limit for a reading at 10 °C is 1.75 Ω.” The question: “(b) Determine the maximum Zs a reading at DBL2 may show on the 15 °C test day, and state whether the readings comply.” Under it: “Give the limit in Ω. The comparison follows.” A typed answer, part 4b. Factor from 10 °C = (15 + 230) ÷ (10 + 230) = 1.02. Limit = 1.75 × 1.02 = 1.785 Ω. Accepted too: 1.786 Ω, from the unrounded factor. Slips: 2.19 Ω, “That is the limit for the cable hot. Set a reading at 15 °C against a cold limit.” 1.716 Ω, “That moves the limit the wrong way. 15 °C is warmer than 10 °C, so the limit goes up.” 1.75 Ω, “That is the limit at 10 °C. Correct it to the 15 °C day.” After two misses, the working. Then: “At DBL2, Ze + (R1+R2) = 0.08 + 0.214 = 0.294 Ω. The direct reading is 0.275 Ω. Both are far under 1.785 Ω, so they comply. The design expected 0.1 + 0.223 = 0.323 Ω. C7's own limit, for its 6 A type C, is 2.91 × 1.02 = 2.968 Ω. At its far end, Ze + (R1+R2) = 0.08 + 0.214 + 0.548 = 0.842 Ω. The direct reading is 0.790 Ω. Both comply with plenty to spare. These cold limits assume cables that run at up to 70 °C. C7 and the submain are 90 °C cables, but they carry a small share of their rating. So they run cool, and the 70 °C limits are fair here. The direct reading comes in 0.052 Ω lower. A direct reading usually does, because it takes in parallel earth paths through bonded metalwork. So never subtract Ze from a direct reading to find R1+R2.”

Screen 8, Section A, question 4 (c). Parts 4(a) and 4(b) carried forward. Said once: “Use Ze + (R1+R2) from the readings, not the direct reading. Ze belongs to the supply, so correct only R1+R2.” The question: “(c) Correct the as-built Zs at C7's farthest bollard to operating temperature, and compare it with the design.” A typed answer, part 4c. R1+R2 = 0.214 + 0.548 = 0.762 Ω at 15 °C. Back to 20 °C: 0.762 ÷ 0.98 = 0.778 Ω. Up to operating temperature: 0.778 × 1.28 = 0.996 Ω. Zs = 0.08 + 0.996 = 1.076 Ω. Also accepted: 1.075 Ω, from unrounded working. Also accepted: 1.078 Ω, using one factor from 15 °C to 90 °C, (90 + 230) ÷ (15 + 230) = 1.31. Slips: 1.055 Ω, “The 1.28 starts from 20 °C. Divide by 0.98 first to bring the reading back to 20 °C.” 1.100 Ω, “You warmed Ze too. Ze belongs to the supply, so correct only R1+R2.” 0.842 Ω, “That is the reading as taken, cold. Correct R1+R2 to operating temperature first.” After two misses, the working. Then: “Like for like, the installation gives 1.076 Ω against the design's 1.129 Ω. That is 0.053 Ω lower, about 5%. Cold against cold, it is 0.842 Ω against the expected 0.887 Ω. That is 0.045 Ω lower. Set the cold reading against the hot design and it looks 0.287 Ω lower. Most of that gap is only temperature. Of the 0.053 Ω gap, 0.02 Ω is Ze. It measured 0.08 Ω against the declared 0.1 Ω. A declared Ze is a maximum, and so are the tabulated resistances. So readings usually come in a little under the design. A reading well over the expected figure means something is wrong. The installation may differ from the design, such as a longer run or a poor connection. Or the test itself went wrong. Find out which.”

Screen 9, Handing over. Two short lists come first, then the interval. Before the tests, the inspector gets five things. Each circuit's expected R1+R2 at the test temperature. Each circuit's maximum permitted Zs, and where it comes from if not Table 41.3. A chart or schedule of each circuit, with its points, its cable size and type, and its protective device. Anything a test could damage, such as SELV equipment. The supply's characteristics. At handover, these go out. The Electrical Installation Certificate, which is valid only with its schedule of inspections and schedules of test results.[^2] The circuit charts and diagrams. The notices, including the periodic inspection notice at the origin. The O&M manual and building log book, where the contract asks for them. On a project under CDM, a copy of the certificate in the health and safety file. Where fixed building services need commissioning, a commissioning notice to building control and the owner. Then the interval: “You recommend the time to the first periodic inspection. It goes on the certificate. The recommended maximum is 5 years for commercial premises and 3 for industrial.[^3] The showroom is commercial, so take 5 years. Shorten it if the building will be poorly maintained or used harder than designed for. Cars on the floor are part of a showroom's normal use. They do not change the 5 years by themselves.”

Screen 10, Section B: “State what decides the maximum period to the showroom's first periodic inspection, and what you would recommend.” It is a written answer, marked against five points. Any three of them make a full answer. There is one more go, then the model answer.

Screen 11, Section B: “List three items of information a designer should give the inspector before the showroom's tests.” It is a written answer, marked against five points. Any three of them make a full answer. There is one more go, then the model answer.

Screen 12, Section A, changed numbers. “A 25 A type C radial circuit is tested on a 20 °C day. It reads Zs 0.74 Ω. Table 41.3 gives 0.87 Ω. Its limit for a reading at 10 °C is 0.70 Ω. Determine the most it may read on the day, and state whether it complies.” A typed answer, in Ω. Factor = (20 + 230) ÷ (10 + 230) = 1.04. Limit = 0.70 × 1.04 = 0.728 Ω. Accepted too: 0.729 Ω, from the unrounded factor. Slips: 0.87 Ω, “That is the limit for the cable hot. Set a cold reading against a cold limit.” 0.673 Ω, “That moves the limit the wrong way. 20 °C is warmer than 10 °C, so the limit goes up.” 0.70 Ω, “That is the limit at 10 °C. Correct it to the 20 °C day.” After it: “0.74 Ω is over 0.728 Ω, so it does not comply. Yet it is under 0.87 Ω. Set against the hot figure, it would have passed. The cold limit scales Ze too, though Ze does not warm with the cable. So it errs a little on the safe side. A reading over it still fails.”

Screen 13, Keep this: the summary card, then Finish the lesson.

Every line is worked from the rounded figures shown before it. Each screen that uses a practice value or an example reading says so.
interactive.ignores: The picture treats the whole cable as one even temperature. It uses a straight-line rule for copper. That is very close over this range, but not exact. It shows R1+R2 only: Ze belongs to the supply and does not follow the cable's temperature. The maximum measured Zs values divide by 1.25. That assumes cables that run at up to 70 °C. The showroom's 90 °C cables carry a small share of their rating, so they run far cooler than that. It also applies copper's rule to the submain's steel armour. Steel's resistance rises a little faster with temperature. But the corrections are made the same way for the design and the readings. So it changes the figures by only a few milliohms.

explain.text:
The design predicts what the installation should read. So verification is a comparison. Each reading is set against the design and against its device's limit. The catch is temperature. The limits are for a fault on a cable already warm from its load. A warm cable has more resistance, so less fault current flows. So the design works R1+R2 and Zs hot. The tests are done cold, with no load on. Set one against the other as they stand and every circuit looks better than it is.

Copper's resistance rises very nearly in step with its temperature plus 230 °C.[^6] So to move a resistance from one temperature to another, multiply by (new + 230) ÷ (old + 230). That one rule gives the factors you use for R1+R2 and Zs. From the 20 °C tables up to 70 °C it is 300 ÷ 250 = 1.20. Up to 90 °C it is 320 ÷ 250 = 1.28. Down to a 15 °C test day it is 245 ÷ 250 = 0.98. The limit for a reading taken cold is the [[maximum measured Zs]]. It is the Table 41.3 figure divided by 1.25.[^9] That is 300 ÷ 240, from 70 °C down to 10 °C. So a cold reading should stay under 80% of the Table 41.3 figure.

Even like for like, readings usually come in a little under the design. The design uses the declared Ze and the largest resistance per metre. Both are maximums. A direct Zs reading also takes in parallel earth paths through bonded metalwork. So it usually reads lower than Ze + (R1+R2).[^20] Never work a direct reading back to find R1+R2.

Then the designer hands over. The inspector gets the expected readings and the limits, before the tests. The client gets the certificate with its schedules, the charts and the records. The certificate carries the designer's recommended interval to the first periodic inspection. For commercial premises the recommended maximum is 5 years.[^3] That closes the showroom job. Its example readings come in within what the design predicted. **Compare a reading with the design, or with a limit, only at the same temperature: move one of them by (t + 230) first.**

analogy.text: Think of tyre pressures. The handbook figure is for a cold tyre. Check after a long motorway run and the gauge reads high, though nothing is wrong. So you check them cold, or you allow for the heat. A cable is the same, the other way round. Its design figures are hot and its test readings cold, so you compare them at one temperature.
analogy.breaks: A tyre warms as it is driven. A cable is warmed by its own load current, so a lightly loaded cable stays close to the room's temperature. And a cable's limit moves too. The maximum measured Zs is the hot limit scaled down by the same rule.

practice.text:
- Before the tests, work each circuit's R1+R2 at 20 °C. To correct it to the expected test temperature, multiply by (t + 230) ÷ 250.
- Add Ze to give the Zs you expect at each far end. Hand these figures to the inspector.
- Take each device's maximum measured Zs at 10 °C. To correct it to the test day, multiply by (t + 230) ÷ 240.
- Record the temperature on the day with the readings.
- Set each reading against its limit to pass or fail it. Set it against the expected figure to check it matches the design.
- To compare with the design's hot figure instead, bring R1+R2 back to 20 °C, then apply the operating multiplier. Leave Ze alone.
- Never subtract Ze from a direct Zs reading to find R1+R2.
- Hand over the certificate with its schedules, the charts, the notices and the records the contract asks for. Enter the recommended interval to the first periodic inspection.

**Rule of thumb:** a cold reading should stay under 80% of the Table 41.3 figure.[^10] Like for like, readings usually come in a little under the design.

**Worked example:** the showroom on a 15 °C day. C7's far end should read 0.1 + 0.223 + 0.564 = 0.887 Ω. Its limit is 2.91 × 1.02 = 2.968 Ω. The example readings give 0.842 Ω. Read directly, it is 0.790 Ω. Corrected to running temperature, 0.842 Ω becomes 1.076 Ω. The design gave 1.129 Ω.

**Common mistakes**
- Setting a cold reading against the Table 41.3 figure.
- Setting a cold reading against the design's hot figure, and calling the gap a margin.
- Moving a limit the wrong way. A warmer test day raises it.
- Correcting Ze along with R1+R2.
- Working a direct Zs reading back to R1+R2.
- Using the maximum measured Zs on a 90 °C cable loaded near its rating. Those values assume 70 °C. Scale its Table 41.3 figure by (t + 230) ÷ 320 instead.

b1.model: As the designer, I recommend the maximum period and enter it on the Electrical Installation Certificate. It allows for how often and how well the showroom will be maintained. It also allows for the type of installation, its use and the external influences on it, such as cars driven across the floor. The recommended maximum for commercial premises such as shops is 5 years. So I would recommend 5 years, or less if maintenance will be poor. It is a recommendation made by engineering judgement and agreed with the installer and others, not a fixed rule.

summary.title: Verification and handover
summary.for: The design predicts what each circuit should read. Compare a reading with the design, or with a limit, only at the same temperature. Before the tests, give the inspector each circuit's expected R1+R2 at the test temperature, its maximum Zs and where that comes from, the charts, anything a test could damage, and the supply's characteristics. At handover, give the client the certificate with its schedules, the charts, the notices and the records.
summary.rule:
R1+R2 is very nearly proportional to (temperature + 230 °C)
Factor from t1 to t2 = (t2 + 230) ÷ (t1 + 230)
Expected R1+R2 on the day = R1+R2 at 20 °C × (t + 230) ÷ 250
Expected Zs = Ze + expected R1+R2
Limit on the day = maximum measured Zs at 10 °C × (t + 230) ÷ 240
Zs hot = Ze + (R1+R2) ÷ test-day factor × operating multiplier

A cold reading should stay under 80% of Table 41.3.
A 90 °C cable near its rating: limit = Table 41.3 figure × (t + 230) ÷ 320.
A direct Zs usually reads lower than Ze + (R1+R2): parallel earth paths.
Like for like, readings usually come in a little under the design.
First periodic inspection: on the certificate. Commercial: 5 years.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the reading bar climb to meet the design's 0.436 Ω at 70 °C, when you drag the cable's temperature up from the 20 °C test day.

applied.problem: Three overreaches: copper's (t + 230) rule is a close straight-line fit, not exact; its own source says a direct Zs usually (not always) reads lower; and the showroom's readings are made-up practice values, so they cannot be described as what verification found.

Screen 7 gives a cause for a gap in invented readings as fact, and screen 8 says a high reading means the installation differs from the design, when a poor connection or a faulty test can also give one.
Parts 4(a) and 4(c) apply copper's (t + 230) rule to the submain's steel armour too; steel's resistance rises a little faster with temperature, and the lesson does not say it has simplified this.
"A tyre is warmed by the road, whatever it carries" is wrong: a tyre heats mainly by flexing, and a heavier load makes it flex and heat more.
The card states resistance as exactly proportional to (temperature + 230 °C); that is the OSG's close straight-line fit for copper, not an exact law, and the card is read on its own.

notes.problem: Dan asked for lessons that explain the content in their own words, not ones telling him where each thing comes from; the screens still carry [^n] markers, the Section B points and traps name sources, and summary.where lists them.
